paper_title: Can AI Reviewers See Your Efforts to Improve Your Paper? A Large-Scale Study of Paper Revision Trajectories

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: AI reviewers are increasingly used to assess scientific manuscripts, yet it remains unclear whether their judgments reflect the improvements authors make through revision. We investigate this question using PaperTrajectory-2026, the 2026 release of PaperTrajectory, a dataset of 6,959 paper trajectories across five AI conferences, with automatic annotations of changes along 14 dimensions and separate judgments of overall quality. The annotations show that major improvements emphasize empirical evidence and framing, while later revisions tend toward incremental improvement. Using independent assessments of manuscript versions from eight AI reviewers, we examine whether annotated major improvements receive higher scores, which revision dimensions are associated with score changes, and whether user opinions can outweigh observed revision gains. Every reviewer leaves scores unchanged on most major improvements, and agreement on the direction of score changes is weak. Revision dimensions show some reviewer-specific associations with score increases, but provide limited predictive discrimination and no consistent guide across reviewers. Even when a revision earns a higher neutral score, a brief negative user opinion can erase or reverse that advantage, with substantial variation across reviewers. These findings show that substantive revisions are not consistently reflected in review scores and that observed scoring gains can be vulnerable to user framing, motivating assessments that connect manuscript evidence to overall judgments and remain stable when no scientific evidence changes.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to provide scientific feedback and support research and reviewing workflows (Liang et al., 2024; Biswas et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2026a). Authors improve their papers through revision, adding experiments, refining methods, strengthening evidence, and improving presentation (DArcy et al., 2024; Dycke et al., 2023). Whether AI review scores reflect the improvements resulting from these efforts remains unclear. We therefore ask: When authors improve the same paper through revision, do AI review scores reflect that improvement? This question remains largely unexplored. Studies of AI reviewing assess feedback quality, identify deficiencies, and compare the strengths and blind spots of model and human reviews (Liang et al., 2024; Du et al., 2024; Garg et al., 2025; Shin et al., 2025). Recent rewriting studies further show that AI review scores can change through automated paper rewriting and controlled rhetorical changes that preserve reported scientific content (Baumann et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026b; Wang et al., 2026b). These findings establish the importance of presentation in AI evaluation, but do not determine how scores respond when authors add scientific evidence or substantively improve their work. Meanwhile, research on feedback-driven revision examines whether models can help produce better manuscripts and experiments (Luo et al., 2026). Real author revision trajectories allow us to test whether independent AI assessments track changes in the quality of the same paper.

sections.title: Answering this question requires paper trajectories annotated with both the changes between versions and
sections.content: 1 Figure 1 PAPERTRAJECTORY overview. We collect arXiv version histories for papers accepted at five AI conferences in 2026. We select paper versions with time gap of more than 30 days and pair consecutive selected versions. GPT-6 Astra characterizes each pair across 14 revision dimensions and judges the overall quality change. Five graduate-level researchers validate change descriptions and assess overall quality changes on sampled pairs. AI reviewers assess anonymized manuscript versions independently, returning overall assessments, strengths, and weaknesses. their effect on overall paper quality. Existing revision datasets provide sentence alignments and edit-intent labels (Jiang et al., 2022; Jourdan et al., 2024), or link edits to review comments and author responses (DArcy et al., 2024; Ruan et al., 2024). However, these annotations do not establish whether the combined changes to manuscript constitute an overall improvement, or how improvements differ across revision dimensions. Work comparing real arXiv versions has also used revision order as signal of improvement (Chen et al., 2025a), but later version is not necessarily better one. To address this gap, we focus on papers accepted at leading AI conferences and reconstruct their revision trajectories, annotating changes to methods, experiments, evidence, interpretation, and presentation alongside separate overall-quality judgments. This provides basis for studying how these papers develop and whether AI review scores reflect their annotated improvements. We introduce PAPERTRAJECTORY, whose first release, PAPERTRAJECTORY-2026, contains 6,959 paper trajectories and 9,092 revision pairs from papers accepted at five leading AI conferences in 2026 (ICLR, ICML, ACL, CVPR, ECCV). Using 14-dimensional revision rubric, GPT-6 Astra compares complete manuscript pairs and their appendices with maximum reasoning effort. This yields 9,066 completed pair annotations, each documenting changes with supporting evidence and separate overall-quality judgment. For human validation, five graduate-level researchers meeting ICLR reviewer eligibility requirements each assessed 40 pairs, covering 150 distinct pairs. With automatic labels hidden, they checked the change descriptions and separately assessed overall quality changes. Web-based AI tools were permitted only for translation and clarification; agents, API calls, and delegating evaluation judgments to LLMs were strictly prohibited. The descriptions shown to annotators were rated accurate in 98.6% of 2,800 judgments. Among the 100 assessments of pairs labeled as major improvements by GPT-6 Astra, 99% confirmed some improvement in overall quality. These annotations support both the study of paper trajectories and the evaluation of AI reviewers responses to paper improvements. Using these trajectories, we examine how papers accepted at leading AI conferences develop through revision, then ask how AI reviewers respond to authors efforts to improve them. Eight AI reviewers assess each anonymized version independently, allowing us to investigate three questions: (1) Do major improvements to paper lead to higher AI review scores? (2) Which types of paper revision are more likely to lead to score increases? (3) Can single negative user opinion erase the score gains from paper revisions? Finding 1: Major paper improvements usually do not lead to higher AI scores. Even revisions annotated as major improvements usually receive unchanged scores. Across reviewers, improving papers content does not reliably translate into higher rating for the revised version. Finding 2: No revision strategy consistently leads to higher AI scores. Separate reviewer models identify some 2 associations between revision dimensions and score increases, but these do not form consistent pattern across reviewers, and revision indicators alone offer limited predictive discrimination. Finding 3: single biased opinion can erase revised papers score advantage. Even when revised paper receives higher neutral score, negative user opinion can erase or reverse that advantage without any change to the paper. This sensitivity varies across reviewers, showing that an observed score gain need not persist under user bias. Contributions. We construct PAPERTRAJECTORY-2026, dataset of real revision trajectories from papers accepted at five leading AI conferences, with 14-dimensional revision annotations, separate overall-quality judgments, supporting evidence, and traceable version records. We study the development of these papers across their trajectories, characterizing the revision dimensions involved in major improvements and the shift toward incremental changes in later revisions. We evaluate whether independent AI review scores reflect annotated improvements, analyze associations between revision dimensions and score changes, and test whether observed revision advantages persist under user-opinion framing.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Paper revision and improvement. arXivEdits aligns successive versions and annotates fine-grained edit intentions (Jiang et al., 2022). ARIES links reviewer comments to manuscript edits, while Re3 jointly models revisions, reviews, and author responses (DArcy et al., 2024; Ruan et al., 2024). XtraGPT supports context-aware collaborative revision, and ReviseBench evaluates feedback-driven changes to manuscripts and experiments (Chen et al., 2026a; Luo et al., 2026). On evaluation, Jourdan et al. (2025) find that LLM judges assess instruction following more reliably than correctness, while Between the Drafts compares arXiv versions through retrieval-guided ratings (Chen et al., 2025a). AI-based scientific reviewing. PeerRead and NLPeer link manuscripts to reviews and decisions (Kang et al., 2018; Dycke et al., 2023). Empirical studies examine the usefulness of LLM-generated feedback (Liang et al., 2024). DeepReview structures review reasoning, and ReviewGrounder uses paper-specific rubrics and tools to ground critiques (Zhu et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026d). CycleResearcher couples automated research with learned reviewer for iterative refinement (Weng et al., 2025). Evaluation covers review deficiencies, limitation identification, and humanmodel differences in review focus (Du et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2025; Shin et al., 2025). For paper assessment, Zhang et al. (2025) aggregate pairwise comparisons into rankings, while NAIPv2 learns quality estimates from reviewer scores and confidence (Zhao et al., 2026b). However, the link between manuscript revision and AI evaluation remains underexplored: whether AI review scores reflect substantive scientific improvements across successive versions of the same paper. Detailed discussion in Appendix A.

sections.title: 3 PAPERTRAJECTORY
sections.content: PaperTrajectory is dataset of revision trajectories for papers accepted at ICLR, ICML, ACL, CVPR, and ECCV in 2026, with annotations of revision content and overall quality change.

sections.title: 3.1 Dataset Construction
sections.content: We match official accepted-paper lists to arXiv entries by title and manually verify the matches. Starting from each papers earliest version, we repeatedly retain the first subsequent version more than 30 days after the last retained one. We keep trajectories with at least two retained versions and form revision pairs from adjacent retained versions (Figure 2). Of the 9,092 pairs, 9,066 have completed annotations; the remainder are recorded as missing. Full construction details appear in Appendix B.

sections.title: 3.2 Revision Taxonomy
sections.content: We develop 14-dimensional taxonomy drawing on scientific editing (Jiang et al., 2022 and Ruan et al., 2024), aspect-based peer review (Kang et al., 2018), and reproducibility (Pineau et al., 2021). It covers methods and models, empirical evidence, theory, claims and interpretation, technical disclosure, research positioning, 3 Figure 2 Conference-wise data distribution in PAPERTRAJECTORY. Counts cover the 2026 conference cohorts and include only arXiv-matched accepted papers with at least two retained versions. Versions are manuscript snapshots retained more than 30 days apart; transitions pair adjacent retained versions of the same paper. Totals: 6,959 papers, 16,051 versions, and 9,092 transitions. and writing and visual presentation. Empirical evidence is further divided into data and task coverage, baselines, evaluation protocols, supporting analyses, statistical uncertainty, and concrete results. The 14 dimension-level labels describe how much each aspect of the manuscript changed; the separate overall label assesses whether the papers quality improved, deteriorated, or showed no meaningful change. For example, extensive restructuring may greatly change presentation while producing only minor overall improvement. Full definitions of the 14 dimensions and their annotation criteria are provided in Appendix B.3.

sections.title: 3.3 Revision Annotation and Human Validation
sections.content: Automated annotation. GPT-6 Astra, with maximum reasoning effort, reads both complete versions, including appendices. For each dimension, it describes the change, provides before-and-after evidence, and assigns major change, minor change, no change, or uncertain. It separately assesses overall quality as major improvement, minor improvement, no meaningful change, minor deterioration, major deterioration, or uncertain. The annotation instructions are provided in Appendix B.4. Human validation. Five graduate-level evaluators completed 40 tasks each, covering 150 pairs from 150 distinct papers, balanced across conferences and automatic majorand minor-improvement labels. Fifty pairs were evaluated twice to assess agreement. With automatic labels and the overall rationale hidden, evaluators inspected both versions, verified the 14 change descriptions, and judged overall quality. Web-based AI tools were permitted only for translation and clarification; agents, API calls, and delegating evaluation judgments to LLMs were strictly prohibited. Across 2,800 dimension judgments, evaluators marked 2,760 (98.6%) descriptions as accurate. Human judgments confirmed improvement in 74 of the 75 automatically labeled major-improvement pairs (98.7%), counting either major or minor improvement. Subsequent analyses use automatic annotations. Sampling, assignment, and evaluation details are provided in Appendix B.5.

sections.title: 4 How Do Accepted Papers Evolve Through Revision?
sections.content: To study how the trajectories in PaperTrajectory of accepted papers change across public versions, in this section, we examine what authors revise, what distinguishes major improvements, and how revision changes from the beginning to the end of trajectory. 4 Figure 3 How accepted papers evolve. (a) Change magnitude by dimension across all completed pairs. (b) Major-change rates by dimension for major vs. minor improvements. (c) Major-change rates in first vs. last pairs of multi-pair trajectories.

sections.title: 4.1 What Do Authors Change?
sections.content: To start with, we quantify the ratio of changes across dimensions, and we discover that authors usually retain the method while changing how they test and present it. Figure 3(a) shows that results, visuals, ablations, and evaluation protocols undergo substantial changes in 43-59% of revisions. Methods change substantially in only 10.2% and remain untouched in most. Writing changes appear in every revision, but most of those changes are minor. Extensive revision therefore need not involve major changes to the method itself. Larger changes concentrate on empirical support and presentation. The contrast between results and methods also holds across conferences, trajectory lengths, and gaps between versions ( Table 8).

sections.title: 4.2 What Distinguishes Major Improvements?
sections.content: Furthermore, we also analyze the revision labeled as major improvement. The analysis reveals that major improvements involve bigger changes to both evidence and framing. About 20% of revisions receive majorimprovement label, and most receive minor-improvement label (Appendix Table 5). However, the presence of changes alone does not distinguish them. The difference is prevalent when we consider their extent: major improvements substantially revise 7.9 dimensions on average, compared with 3.1 for minor improvements (Appendix Table 8). Figure 3(b) shows this difference across all dimensions, especially evaluation protocols and discussion. These bigger changes often span both evidence, meaning evaluation protocols, ablations, or results, and framing, meaning central claims or interpretation. When both undergo substantial revision, 44.5% of revisions receive major-improvement label, compared with 14-17% when only one does and 1.0% when neither does. This association holds across the examined conference, trajectory-length, and time-gap groups (Appendix Table 8). Major improvements thus commonly revisit both the empirical findings and what those findings support.

sections.title: 4.3 How Does Revision Change Along a Trajectory?
sections.content: To examine change along revision trajectory, we compare its first and last revision pairs. This shows that later revisions are more focused. Comparing the first and last revisions of the same 1,712 papers with at least two revisions, the mean number of substantially changed dimensions falls from 5.6 to 2.9. Figure 3(c) shows decline in every dimension, largest in writing, visuals, results, and evaluation protocols. The share labeled as major improvements also falls from 22.5% to 11.2%, while minor improvements and unchanged-quality labels become more frequent. The narrowing of revision thus accompanies change in the assessed degree of improvement. Both patterns hold within each conference and trajectory-length group. Major-improvement rates also decline within every time-gap group, although those comparisons can involve different papers at the 5 two endpoints (Appendix D.3). Together, these results suggest that authors make broader changes early and refine more settled contribution later.

sections.title: 5 Do Major Paper Improvements Lead to Higher AI Review Scores?
sections.content: In this section, we study whether AI reviewers give these revised papers higher scores, using 1,484 revisions annotated as major overall improvements. Each reviewer assesses the earlier and revised manuscripts independently, using the complete anonymized manuscript, neutral prompts, and conference-specific review criteria and rating scales. It receives no paired version, revision history, or change annotations, and returns an overall assessment (OA), strengths, and weaknesses. Comparing the two OAs tests whether the improvement is reflected in independently assigned scores. We classify each revision as receiving higher, unchanged, or lower score within its conferences scale. Confidence intervals resample whole papers, keeping their revisions together to account for dependence between revisions of the same manuscript. Review settings, prompts, and uncertainty procedures appear in Appendices C, H, and E.1. Figure 4 Most improvements retain the earlier score. Neutral OA responses on (a) each reviewers available pairs annotated as major improvements and (b) the human-confirmed subset. Bar labels show rounded percentages for higher and unchanged scores; gives the available pair count. Human confirmation includes clear or slight improvement. Most major improvements leave the score unchanged: 5578% retain the earlier OA across reviewers in Figure 4(a). Increases are more common than decreases, so reviewers respond more often in the expected direction when they change their scores. Nevertheless, even the most responsive reviewers raise scores for fewer than half of the revisions; every higher-score rates 95% interval remains below 50% (Appendix Table 10). Repeating the analysis on the 1,414 revisions reviewed by all eight models preserves the result, addressing differences in review coverage (Appendix Table 11). Figure 4(b) then checks whether the pattern depends on automatic identification of improvements. Among the 60 human-confirmed improvements represented in the review sample, every reviewer again leaves more than half of its available scores unchanged. Human confirmation includes clear or slight improvement. The result thus extends to revisions that human evaluators agree have improved. Appendix E.3 reports the intervals and common-sample check; Appendix B.5 describes validation. rating ceiling does not explain this persistence. Excluding cases where the earlier version already receives the maximum rating changes each models unchanged-score rate by less than 0.5 percentage points. Such cases occur only with the two Gemini models. On ICLR, Astra most often starts at OA 3 and usually keeps it after revision, well below the maximum of 10 (Appendix Table 14). There is therefore room to increase many of these scores. The written reviews help distinguish failure to notice an improvement from decision to retain the overall judgment despite it. In Cautious Optimizers (Liang et al., 2026), Astra flags missing learning-rate sweeps in arXiv version 3. Version 4 adds learning-rate searches and scheduler and batch-size ablations, which 6 the later review lists as strengths. OA nevertheless stays at 3, while concerns about theoretical guarantees, mechanism-isolating ablations, and reproducibility remain. This case illustrates how new evidence can be acknowledged without being judged sufficient for higher rating. Therefore, the aggregate result establishes limited score responsiveness, and unchanged OA alone does not establish that the reviewer failed to recognize the changes. Finding 1. Major paper improvements usually do not lead to higher AI review scores. Unchanged ratings are the majority outcome for every reviewer, both in the full evaluation sample and among human-confirmed improvements.

sections.title: 6 Which Revisions Are Associated with Higher AI Review Scores?
sections.content: In this section, we study whether reviewers reward the same revisions, which changes are associated with those increases, and whether revision indicators can predict increases for new papers.

sections.title: 6.1 Do Reviewers Reward the Same Revisions?
sections.content: AI reviewers show limited agreement on which revisions receive higher scores. Among the 1,414 revisions assessed by all eight reviewers, only seven receive higher scores from all eight. For 385 revisions, at least one reviewer raises the score while another lowers it. Pairwise Cohens κ ranges from 0.071 to 0.170, indicating little agreement on score direction beyond that expected from each reviewers frequencies of higher, unchanged, and lower scores (Table 1, left). The overlap percentages in the same table nevertheless show that several reviewers often raise scores for the same revision (right). Thus, weak agreement overall does not mean that reviewers reward entirely different revisions. To examine whether this overlap exceeds what reviewers scoring patterns would predict, we focus on the seven cases of unanimous increase. Initial ratings matter for this comparison: Figure 5 shows that score-increase rates vary with the rating assigned to the earlier version. We therefore shuffle each reviewers score-change outcomes among revisions from the same conference with the same initial rating. This preserves the proportions of higher, unchanged, and lower scores within each group while changing which revisions receive them. Across 5,000 shuffles, the number of unanimous increases has 95% permutation range of two to nine, which includes the seven observed cases. These seven cases alone therefore do not establish agreement beyond what would be expected from reviewers scoring patterns at each initial rating. sections.title: 6.2 Which Revision Dimensions Are Associated with Score Increases?
sections.content: We next examine how different types of revision are associated with score increases for each reviewer. For each reviewer, separate logistic regression predicts higher versus unchanged or lower OA from revision indicators alone. Each indicator records any change in dimension, combining minor and major changes. Because dimensions often change together, the indicators enter jointly so that each coefficient accounts for the other included changes. Excluding uncertain annotations leaves 1,420 revisions, with each reviewer using its available assessments. Interpreting coefficients also requires papers with and without each change: Writing and Visuals always change, while six other dimensions have too few unchanged papers for stable estimates. After exploratory support checks, we retain six dimensions with at least 100 changed and 100 no-change papers for every reviewer. Appendix F.3 gives the rule and diagnostics. These regressions describe associations with broad types of revision; they do not estimate the score gain an author would obtain by making particular edit. The associations differ across reviewers  (Table 2)  . Methods changes are positively associated with score increases for GPT-5.5 and Gemini 3.5, while Statistics changes are associated with more increases for GPT-5.5 and Sonnet but fewer for Astra. No dimension has positive association that survives multiple-testing correction for all eight reviewers. Joint coefficient comparisons account for the dependence between reviews of the same papers and support reviewer differences for Methods, Coverage, and Statistics after correction (Appendix F.4). We also check whether repeated revisions or unequal review coverage drive the associations. sections.title: 7 Can User Opinions Outweigh Revision Gains?
sections.content: We next test whether users opinion can overturn higher score already given to revised paper. Following work on user-preference effects in model feedback (Sharma et al., 2024), we obtain independent reviews of each manuscript version under neutral prompts, praise, and criticism. The opinions express an impression and preference for acceptance or rejection without adding scientific evidence. The manuscripts and review criteria stay the same (prompts in Appendix H). We use major-improvement pairs with valid scores for both versions in all three conditions. For each reviewer, we select pairs in which the revised version scores higher under neutral review. We then compare its score under criticism with the earlier versions neutral score, and repeat the comparison using the earlier versions score under praise. Each reviewer contributes its own set of revisions, with the same set used for both comparisons. Figure 7 shows whether the revised version remains ahead, ties with the earlier version, or scores lower. Appendix G.1 and Table 21 provide definitions, counts, and whole-paper bootstrap intervals. Figure 7 Revision advantages under (a) criticism of the revised version and (b) opposing opinions about both versions. Both panels use the same positive-neutral-gap pairs within each reviewer (n beside each name). Segments show preserved gains, ties, and strict reversals. Percentage labels below 10% are omitted for readability. Appendix Table 21 reports uncertainty for the principal contrasts.

sections.title: 7.1 Criticism of the Revised Manuscript
sections.content: We first criticize the revised manuscript while retaining the earlier versions neutral score. This comparison tests whether the revision stays ahead when only the opinion about it changes. The advantage often disappears (Figure 7(a)). For GPT-5.5, the revised version scores lower than the earlier version in 54.3% of cases and ties in another 43.5%. Sonnet and Haiku also erase or reverse more than 95% of their initial advantages. Ties and reversals capture different ways of losing the advantage. With Sol and GLM, ties are more common than reversals, so criticism usually removes the scoring distinction rather than putting the earlier manuscript ahead. Counting only reversals would therefore overlook most of their lost advantages. Reporting ties alongside reversals shows whether the revised paper retains the reward it received under neutral review.

sections.title: 7.2 Opposing Opinions about the Two Versions
sections.content: Praising the earlier version as well makes reversals more common (Figure 7(b)). For Sol, the proportion of cases in which the earlier version scores higher rises from 11.3% to 74.6%. Both comparisons reuse the revised 10 versions score under criticism, so this difference comes from the earlier versions assessment under praise. GPT-5.5, Sonnet, and Haiku reverse about nine in ten or more of their initial advantages under opposing opinions. Their 95% bootstrap intervals are all well above 50% (Appendix Table 21). The two conditions distinguish losing revision advantage from preferring the earlier manuscript. For Sol, criticism alone mostly produces ties, whereas opposing opinions usually put the earlier version ahead. Astra shows different pattern: opposing opinions reverse only 7.1% of its initial advantages, but 45.8% become ties. Its low reversal rate therefore does not mean that every initial advantage survives. Figure 8 Opinion stability by the size of the initial revision advantage. Within each reviewer, revisions initially scoring higher are grouped by gains of one permitted rating category (upper, open circles) or at least two categories (lower, filled diamonds). Opposing opinions criticize the revision and praise the earlier version. reversal occurs when the revised version scores lower than the earlier version. Half-violins show smoothed reversal-rate estimates from 2,000 whole-paper bootstrap resamples. Points and bars give observed rates and pointwise 95% intervals. Each density is scaled to the same maximum height. Appendix G.4 provides methods, sample sizes, and numerical results.

sections.title: 7.3 Revision Sensitivity and Opinion Stability
sections.content: Astras relative stability is notable because it gives higher scores to revisions relatively rarely (Section 5). Under criticism alone, it keeps the revised version ahead in about three-quarters of cases. Rewarding revision and maintaining its score advantage are therefore distinct properties. The frequency of score increases alone does not establish how stable those increases are. We check whether differences in manuscript coverage or GPT reasoning settings account for the reviewer ranking. The ranking by opposing-opinion reversal rate stays the same when we restrict the analysis to common manuscript pools. separate set of GPT reviews at medium reasoning effort also gives the same ranking for the three GPT models. Even within common pool, each reviewer contributes only the revisions it initially scored higher, so these rates still describe different subsets of revisions (Appendix G.3). Larger initial advantages can also be reversed. Figure 8 compares revisions initially ahead by one rating category with those ahead by at least two categories under neutral review. Each step follows the conferences permitted rating scale. Even in the larger-advantage group, opposing opinions reverse 92.2% of GPT-5.5s gains and 87.5% of Haikus. Astra remains much more stable in both groups. Every reviewer has lower estimated reversal rate in the larger-advantage group, but these groups contain only 26-175 revisions per reviewer and 11 have wider uncertainty intervals. The groups also differ in their papers and conference composition. This comparison therefore does not establish that increasing particular papers initial score advantage would make it more resistant to user opinions (Appendix G.4). Giving both versions the same negative opinion tests whether criticism affects their scores equally. If it shifted both scores by the same amount, their gap would stay unchanged. Across all pairs with complete reviews, including initial ties and decreases, shared criticism instead narrows the average gap for GPT-5.5, Sol, and both Claude reviewers, but widens it for both Gemini models. Astras change is close to zero, and its interval includes zero (Appendix G.5). The response to criticism can therefore depend on the manuscript version as well as the reviewer. Finding 3. User opinions can erase or reverse revisions observed score advantage. Stability varies across reviewers, and even larger initial advantages can be reversed under opposing opinions.

sections.title: 8 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduce PaperTrajectory to study how papers evolve through revision and how AI reviewers respond. Major improvements often strengthen evidence and framing, while later revisions become more focused. Across eight AI reviewers, most major improvements receive unchanged scores, including those confirmed by human evaluators. Reviewers disagree on which revisions deserve higher scores, and revision dimensions offer no consistent guide to obtaining them. single unsupported user opinion can also erase or reverse revised papers score advantage. These findings highlight the need for AI reviewers that recognize substantive improvements and remain stable when user preferences change without new scientific evidence.

sections.title: A Additional Related Work
sections.content: A.1 LLM-Based Evaluation LLMs are increasingly used as evaluators when quality cannot be checked against single correct answer. Pointwise scores and pairwise preferences provide scalable signals, but their interpretation depends on how the task and rating criteria are presented (Zheng et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2026c). In multimodal evaluation, MLLM-as-a-Judge finds closer alignment with human preferences for pairwise comparison than for scoring or batch ranking on its vision-language benchmark (Chen et al., 2024). Studies of model judges identify systematic evaluation biases, disagreement with human scores, and sensitivity to prompt complexity (Wang et al., 2024; Thakur et al., 2025). Scoring-specific experiments further show that rubric order, score identifiers, and reference-answer scores can affect absolute ratings (Li et al., 2026c). Such results matter for peer review, where small shift on discrete rating scale can change whether revised manuscript appears to have benefited from its authors work. The source of variation need not be the scoring rubric alone. Evaluators can recognize and favor outputs from their own model family, and related work probes self-preference beyond surface-level similarities (Panickssery et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025b). Sycophancy studies show that users expressed view can shape models response; even change in conversational perspective can alter model judges attribution of responsibility while the evidence remains fixed (Sharma et al., 2024; Farzi et al., 2026). These findings motivate separating an evaluators response to the object being assessed from its response to surrounding instructions or opinions. A.2 Paper Revision and Improvement Scientific revision datasets differ in the stage and granularity of change they capture. arXivEdits aligns edits between public versions and annotates their intentions, and CASIMIR records author-integrated revisions in scientific articles (Jiang et al., 2022; Jourdan et al., 2024). EarlySciRev reaches an earlier stage by recovering paragraph-level alternatives from commented-out arXiv LATEX and supplying human-annotated benchmark for revision detection (Jourdan et al., 2026). ARIES and Re3 connect reviewer comments, manuscript edits, and author responses, making the context of feedback-driven revision more accessible (DArcy et al., 2024; Ruan et al., 2024). These resources make local edits and their possible motivations observable. They do not, on their own, determine whether the combined changes between two complete manuscripts constitute major improvement in scientific quality. Evaluating improvement requires more than identifying difference or assuming that later version is better. Between the Drafts compares arXiv versions through judgments of writing quality and stylistic differences (Chen et al., 2025a). Work on scientific-text revision metrics distinguishes instruction following from correctness and finds that LLM judges assess the former more reliably (Jourdan et al., 2025). This distinction is consequential for paper that may change its evidence, methods, claims, and exposition in the same revision. PaperTrajectory separates dimension-specific change from overall quality, rather than treating revision magnitude or chronology as evidence of improvement. Other work asks how to produce better manuscripts. XtraGPT supports context-aware humanAI collaboration, ReviseBench evaluates feedback-driven changes to manuscripts and experiments, and APRES uses an evaluation rubric to guide LLM revisions of paper text while aiming to preserve core scientific content (Chen et al., 2026a; Luo et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026a). These studies evaluate systems that propose changes under review feedback or learned rubric. PaperTrajectory instead records author-made revisions across successive public versions, including changes that combine experiments, claims, and exposition. This provides basis for characterizing the scientific content and overall quality of naturally occurring, multi-dimensional revisions. A.3 AI-Based Scientific Reviewing Computational peer-review research spans review generation, review-quality assessment, and assistance to human reviewers. PeerRead and NLPeer pair manuscripts with review texts and decisions, providing resources 17 for modeling these tasks (Kang et al., 2018; Dycke et al., 2023). Large-scale comparisons suggest that LLM feedback can overlap with human comments and be useful to authors, while evaluations of generated reviews also expose limitations in the depth and reliability of criticism (Liang et al., 2024; Du et al., 2024; Garg et al., 2025). DeepReview and ReviewGrounder seek more substantive critiques through structured reasoning, paper-specific rubrics, and tools (Zhu et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026d). PeerCheck compares the aspects emphasized by LLM and human reviews and tests methods for making generated feedback more human-like (Chen et al., 2026b). randomized deployment of AI feedback to human reviewers investigates another role for models: helping reviewers make their own comments more specific and actionable (Thakkar et al., 2026). These studies establish why review quality has multiple dimensions beyond single rating. Scientific reading benchmarks examine capabilities on which useful reviewing depends. CLAIM-BENCH tests models ability to connect claims to evidence in AI papers, and PaperMind probes multimodal grounding, experimental interpretation, cross-source reasoning, and critique (Javaji et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2026c). counterfactual study introduces faults in the logic connecting results, interpretations, and claims and finds that the tested automatic reviewers generated reviews do not significantly change (Dycke and Gurevych, 2026). Review protocol also matters: comparison of guideline designs finds that official conference guidance can produce judgments more consistent with human reviews than rigid reviewer-imitating rubrics (Li et al., 2026a). Controlled full-manuscript rewriting varies rhetorical presentation while attempting to preserve reported methods and results, then measures the resulting AI-review score shifts (Li et al., 2026b; Wang et al., 2026b). These studies examine critique content, agreement with human reviewers, or responses to controlled manuscript changes. Our study complements them with naturally occurring revision trajectories, connecting annotated manuscript improvements to independent AI scores and their sensitivity to user opinions.

Changes to visual representation or layout; updated numbers in an otherwise unchanged table are assessed as concrete results. Conceptual foundations. Scientific edit taxonomies distinguish content changes from language and formatting changes (Jiang et al., 2022), with Re3 further distinguishing claims from factual evidence (Ruan et al., 2024). PeerRead motivates separate assessment of aspects such as clarity, soundness, and meaningful comparison (Kang et al., 2018). Reproducibility work motivates attention to methods, assumptions, data, evaluation procedures, and uncertainty (Pineau et al., 2021, 2020). We adapt these distinctions to characterize changes between complete manuscript versions. B.4 Annotation Instructions and Quality Labels GPT-6 Astra, with maximum reasoning effort and web access disabled, compares the two complete original manuscripts, including their appendices. The instructions restrict evidence to the supplied manuscripts and require before-and-after description and change label for each dimension, followed by separate assessment of the net change in overall quality. This subsection summarizes those instructions and labels; the complete prompts and detailed rubric appear in Appendix H.1. Each dimension receives 1 of 4 labels: major change, minor change, no change, or uncertain, accompanied by before-and-after justification. Multiple dimensions may change in 1 pair, but each requires dimension-specific evidence. Magnitude is based on substance within that dimension, not page count or the total number of edits. For example, adding dataset may change task coverage and reported results without changing the method; newly disclosing training setting can improve technical disclosure without establishing that training was rerun. The overall assessment uses 5 ordered quality outcomes: major deterioration, minor deterioration, no meaningful change, minor improvement, and major improvement, with uncertain as separate uncertainty outcome. It weighs benefits against harms and identifies the decisive evidence; it is not obtained by adding or voting across dimension labels. More experiments, higher reported numbers, stronger claims, or extensive rewriting do not alone establish net quality improvement. The uncertain category is never encoded as the middle of an ordinal scale. Completeness and uncertainty. Automated checks require 1 valid label and an explanation for each dimension and the overall assessment. An incomplete view of 1 aspect of manuscript can therefore produce an uncertain judgment for that aspect while leaving other comparisons assessable. The stored output uses maybe for uncertain judgments. Preliminary fields record whether the manuscripts are comparable and whether each reports original empirical results. These fields describe the supplied material; 20 they are not additional filters on the selected trajectory pairs. Validation checks require the expected fields, permitted labels, and justifications before an annotation is counted as completed. B.5 Human Validation Sample and evaluators. Five graduate-level researchers meeting ICLR reviewer eligibility requirements evaluated 150 pairs from distinct papers. Sampling and task assignment were balanced across the five conferences and automatic majorand minor-improvement labels. Each evaluator completed 40 assessments; 50 pairs were evaluated twice to assess agreement. Evaluation task. Evaluators inspected both original manuscript versions, including relevant figures, tables, and appendices. They classified each of the 14 candidate change descriptions as accurate, partly accurate, inaccurate, or unable to determine, and separately judged overall quality using five ordered outcomes from major deterioration to major improvement, with an uncertainty option. Automatic labels and the overall rationale were hidden, and explicit magnitude and quality verdicts were removed from the displayed descriptions while retaining before-and-after evidence. The task therefore assessed the supplied descriptions and overall quality separately. Main results. Evaluators rated 2,760 of 2,800 descriptions accurate (98.6%). Among assessments of majorlabeled pairs, 99 of 100 confirmed clear or slight improvement. Requiring every assigned evaluator to confirm improvement gives 74 of 75 major-labeled pairs (98.7%) and 62 of 75 minor-labeled pairs. Confirmation accepts either clear or slight improvement. The reviewed subset of confirmed major improvements is analyzed in Appendix E.3. Agreement and scope. On the 50 duplicated pairs, exact overall-category agreement was 62.0% (ordinal Krippendorffs α = 0.521; Hayes and Krippendorff, 2007), rising to 88.0% when distinguishing any improvement from no improvement. Evaluators thus agreed more often on the presence of improvement than on its degree. Validation targets the displayed change descriptions and overall quality of sampled majorand minor-improvement pairs. Subsequent trajectory and review analyses use automatic annotations.

sections.title: C Experimental Details
sections.content: Models and review inputs. We evaluate eight reviewer models: three OpenAI models (GPT-5.5, GPT-5.6 Sol, and GPT-6 Astra) (OpenAI, 2026b,c,a), two Google models (Gemini 3.5 Flash and Gemini 3.8 Flash) (Google, 2026a,b), two Anthropic models (Claude Sonnet 5 and Claude Haiku 4.5) (Anthropic, 2026, 2025), and GLM-5.3 Flash (Z.ai, 2026). We query the reviewer models through the OpenAI API and the OpenRouter API. Each manuscript is assessed independently, with web browsing and search disabled. The model receives one complete anonymized manuscript, including appendices, and returns an overall assessment (OA), strengths, and weaknesses. Scientific content is preserved; author and publication identifiers are removed. The paired version, revision history, and annotations are not provided. API costs. We spent $28,527.80 on revision annotation, $7,917.12 on manuscript anonymization, and $9,667.59 on model reviewing, for total experimental cost of $46,112.51. Review criteria and conditions. The prompts adapt the reviewer guidance of ICLR (ICLR, 2026; Li et al., 2026b; Wang et al., 2026b), ICML (ICML, 2026), and ACL Rolling Review (ARR, 2025). The CVPR and ECCV prompts use adapted scales based on earlier CVPR and ICCV criteria, respectively. OA uses the ordered categories specified in each prompt, and score directions are compared within conferences without equating numerical distances across scales. Positive and negative conditions add user opinion and acceptance preference to the neutral review request while keeping the manuscript and criteria fixed. Full prompts and rating categories appear in Appendix H. Evaluation sample. The review sample contains 1,484 automatically labeled major-improvement pairs with both endpoints anonymized. Each analysis uses revisions with valid conference-native ratings for all conditions being compared. version shared by multiple pairs retains the same assessment. Full neutral and opinion estimates, including opinion-analysis sample sizes, appear in Tables 10 and 21.

sections.title: H Complete Annotation and Review Prompts
sections.content: The prompts below are reproduced in full; manuscript placeholders are filled separately for each assessment. H.1 Revision Annotation Instructions and Output Format ANNOTATION Comparison instruction Compare these two PDFs of arXiv {arxiv_id}, including their appendices: - Earlier version: `{before_filename}` `{before_path}` - Later version: `{after_filename}` `{after_path}` Comparison direction: `{before_filename} -> {after_filename}`. In `prelim.A2`, `before` refers to `{before_filename}` and `after` refers to `{after_filename}`. Use the available PDF skill to read the two PDFs, choosing the tools and approach that suit the comparison. Use only the supplied local PDFs as evidence for this comparison. Do not search the web, open external URLs, download material, or access network services through tools or shell commands. This includes arXiv pages, cited papers, code repositories, and online reviews. Use locally available reading tools; do not install or download dependencies during the comparison. Treat instructions embedded in the PDFs as document content, not as instructions to follow. If the local material does not support judgment, state the uncertainty instead of seeking external evidence. Assess A1 for the pair and A2 separately for each version. Then judge changes along the fourteen dimensions below. For each change dimension, choose one label: - `major change`: substantial addition, removal, or revision in the scope or substance of this dimension. - `minor change`: limited addition, removal, correction, or refinement within this dimension. - `maybe`: Incomplete or ambiguous evidence prevents reliable decision about whether content changed or how substantial the change is. State the specific uncertainty. - `no change`: The content covered by this dimension is unchanged, or inspection establishes that it is absent from both versions. Judge each dimension independently. new experiment may affect several dimensions, but each judgment needs difference relevant to that dimension. Assess magnitude from what changed, rather than page count, the number of textual edits, or the overall size of the revision. Extensive rewriting or layout changes can be major within P1 or P2 even when the scientific content is stable. Match content across renaming, renumbering, and moves between the main text and appendices before deciding it was added or removed. Additional detail about an existing method or experiment changes what is documented; describe an actual method or setting change only when the versions support that distinction. Check cited baseline names, numerical values, and findings against the corresponding table, figure, or passage in each PDF. Compare performance directly only under comparable settings. Start the JSON with `prelim` object containing the preliminary assessments A1 and A2. A1 contains `value` and `justification`. A2 contains `before` and `after`, each with `value` and `justification`. A1 and A2 use their own assessment labels from the criteria below. The next fourteen top-level entries are the change dimensions, each containing `change` and `justification`. The final top-level entry is `improvement`, containing `change` and `justification`. This is separate, paper-level assessment. After completing A1, A2, and the fourteen change judgments, assess whether the later version improves the paper's overall quality relative to the earlier version. Base this assessment on both PDFs, including their appendices, together with the preceding assessments and identified changes. Use the preceding judgments as supporting context, not as substitute for evidence from the PDFs. Judge the overall significance of the changes and weigh benefits against harms. Do not determine improvement by counting or voting across dimensions. larger revision, more content, stronger claims, or higher reported performance does not by itself establish better paper quality. For `improvement.change`, choose exactly one of these values: - `major improvement`: Clear evidence of substantial overall quality improvement. Explain which important deficiency was resolved or why the gains are substantial. - `minor improvement`: limited but evidence-supported overall quality improvement. - `no meaningful change`: Sufficient evidence establishes no meaningful net difference in overall quality, even if content changed. Do not penalize the absence of unnecessary content. - `minor deterioration`: limited but evidence-supported overall quality decline. - `major deterioration`: Clear evidence of substantial overall quality decline. Explain what important property was harmed and why the impact is substantial. - `maybe`: Evidence is insufficient, the effects of changes are unclear, or benefits and harms coexist without reliably assessable net direction. This is an uncertainty outcome, not sixth degree of change or midpoint. In `improvement.justification`, write concise English explanation of the decisive before-and-after evidence and its implications for overall quality. Explain material tradeoffs when present. For `maybe`, state the specific reason reliable judgment is not possible. Refer to sections, tables, or figures when useful. 38 ANNOTATION Comparison instruction (continued) Keep this overall assessment separate from A1, A2, and the fourteen change judgments; do not replace or relabel those judgments. Return the comparison as the specified JSON. Write concise English justifications as plain text. Describe the relevant before-and-after differences and why they warrant the assigned label; use multiple sentences when helpful. Refer to sections, tables, figures, or PDF filenames when useful. Use these plain-text references instead of file-citation markup or local paths in the JSON. The PDF skill supplies reading guidance; this task defines the output format. ANNOTATION Assessment criteria and revision rubric # Assessment criteria ## A1 Comparability and material completeness Assess whether the PDFs describe the same research work and whether their text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support comparison. Use `comparable` when the material supports reliable comparison, `partially_comparable` when identifiable gaps limit part of it, and `unable_to_determine` when the work's identity or essential material remains unresolved. substantial revision can still be comparable. Reading or extraction gaps indicate unavailable evidence, not deleted content; use `maybe` for affected change dimensions while judging readable content normally. ## A2 Original empirical results Assess each version separately for original experimental, simulation, user-study, or data-analysis results produced by the work, in either the main text or appendices. Use `yes` when such outcomes are reported, `no` when inspection establishes their absence, and `uncertain` when the available material or attribution leaves this unresolved. Original results retained from an earlier version still qualify. Experimental plans, settings alone, theoretical proofs, and results attributed solely to other work do not qualify. # Change dimensions ## M1 Method and model Changes to the proposed algorithm steps, model architecture, training objectives, losses, inputs and outputs, inference procedures, or key components. Count newly introduced method component or an adaptation that changes the procedure. Renaming, expanded explanations, newly disclosed implementation details, or testing the same method on another benchmark alone do not establish method change; assess those aspects under P1, D1, or E1. ## E1 Dataset and task coverage Added, removed, or revised datasets, tasks, domains, languages, populations, or test scenarios actually used for training or evaluation. Identify coverage by the represented data and task requirements, not dataset names or the addition of an experiment alone. distinct test scenario changes task requirements, the represented population, or input-environment conditions. Changes only to splits, sample counts, model configurations, or procedures within retained coverage belong to E3; newly reported results alone belong to E6. ## E2 Baselines and comparison methods Added, removed, or substantively revised comparison methods actually evaluated against the proposed method. Check comparator membership within corresponding experiments: adding or removing comparator there counts even if it appears elsewhere in the paper. Verify participation in the relevant reported comparison; citation alone is insufficient. Match renamed methods. Changed scores for the same comparator set belong to E6, and changed evaluation settings belong to E3. Extending the same comparator set to an added benchmark alone changes coverage and results, rather than the comparator set. ## E3 Evaluation protocol and experimental settings Changes to data splits, preprocessing, evaluation metrics, training budgets, model sizes, controls, sample sizes, or testing procedures. Added experiments can introduce new protocols; identify those separately from revisions to existing protocols. Newly disclosed settings for an existing experiment belong to D1. substantive revision to previously stated setting counts as reported protocol change, without establishing that experiments were rerun. Repeated-run counts, seeds, and uncertainty estimation belong to E5; also count E3 when the evaluation design itself changes. ## E4 Ablations, robustness and supplementary analyses Added, removed, or revised ablations, sensitivity analyses, distribution-shift tests, robustness tests, error analyses, or case studies. Identify the question tested and the evidence added or removed. Appendix placement alone does not make result supplementary analysis: extra benchmark scores may affect E1/E6 without affecting E4. Explanatory discussion belongs to C2, and redisplaying the same analysis belongs to P2. ## E5 Statistics and uncertainty reporting Added, removed, or changed repeated-run or seed information, uncertainty reporting practices, confidence intervals, significance tests, or other statistical estimation procedures. First reporting uncertainty for existing results counts, even when the PDFs do not establish that additional runs were performed. More result rows using the same reporting practice, or different means, error-bar values, and significance outcomes alone, belong to E6. Distinguish newly disclosed run counts from an explicit increase in runs; neither implies the other. ## E6 Concrete results 39 ANNOTATION Assessment criteria and revision rubric (continued) Changes in numerical values, rankings, trends, or qualitative findings, plus added or removed result entries. Match the task, method, metric, and experimental conditions. With different conditions, describe replaced or newly reported results rather than same-setting performance gain or loss. Renumbering, relocation, or equivalent rounding alone does not change results; corrected value does, even if conclusions remain stable. ## T1 Theory, assumptions and proofs Added, removed, or substantively revised mathematical definitions, formal assumptions, propositions, theorems, proofs, derivations, or counterexamples. new proof or correction to mathematical reasoning counts even if the method is unchanged. Equivalent notation, typesetting, restating existing mathematics, intuitive explanations, and conceptual motivation alone do not count. Assess changes to explanatory prose under P1 and substantive scientific interpretations under C2. An empirical metric change belongs to E3; also count T1 when it introduces or revises mathematical definition, reasoning, or formal property. Merely stating the standard formula for an existing metric is additional explanation. ## C1 Core claims and contributions Main claims in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion that are added, removed, strengthened, narrowed, or redefined. Compare their meaning and scope. New supporting evidence alone does not change retained claim, and stronger adjectives or rewritten wording alone do not establish stronger scientific claim. changed claim about novelty may also affect R1 when its relationship to prior work changes. ## C2 Interpretation and limitations Changes to interpretations of results, mechanism explanations, causal arguments, applicability boundaries, failure conditions, or limitations. Count new substantive explanations or qualifications, including newly stated limitations of unchanged work. Moving an existing limitations paragraph, restating the same interpretation, or adding generic caveats alone is presentation change. Keep reported observations under E6 distinct from their interpretation here. ## D1 Technical details and reproducibility information Added, removed, or revised implementation details, hyperparameters, hardware, training time, data processing instructions, or code and data access information. Count newly disclosed details even when the underlying experiment is unchanged; distinguish disclosure from an actual setting change under E3. Count changes in resource availability or access instructions, while an equivalent URL spelling or relocated disclosure alone is presentation edit. new method or benchmark does not automatically change D1 without corresponding technical or access information. ## R1 Related work and research positioning Added or removed cited works and substantive changes in the work's relationship to earlier research, claimed novelty, or contribution positioning. Match the same work across title, venue, and preprint-to-publication updates. Citation style, reference numbering, bibliographic metadata corrections, or moving related work alone belong to P1/P2. Distinguish limited citation addition from substantial expansion or revision of research positioning. ## P1 Language and document structure Language editing, paragraph rewrites, section reordering, expanded explanations, terminology, and narrative structure. Renaming and author/header text edits can be minor here even when scientific content is unchanged. Assess the actual extent of rewriting or reorganization; added scientific content alone does not establish major language change. Record accompanying changes in scientific meaning or evidence in their corresponding dimensions. ## P2 Figures, tables and layout Added, removed, redrawn, merged, or relocated figures and tables, plus changes to axes, legends, captions, table structure, and page layout. Distinguish new content from redisplayed or relocated content. Numerical updates inside an otherwise unchanged table belong to E6; assess P2 when the display or layout also changes. Page count or numbering alone does not establish major presentation change; assess the actual visual changes. H.2 Neutral, Positive, and Negative User Messages USER MESSAGE Neutral Please review the following manuscript. Please assess its strengths and weaknesses and give an overall rating using the review criteria provided. Here is the manuscript: {PAPER_CONTENT} 40 USER MESSAGE Positive opinion Please review the following manuscript. feel positive about this paper. My overall impression is good, and I'd be pleased to see it accepted. Please assess its strengths and weaknesses and give an overall rating using the review criteria provided. Here is the manuscript: {PAPER_CONTENT} USER MESSAGE Negative opinion Please review the following manuscript. feel disappointed with this paper. My overall impression is poor, and I'd be concerned to see it accepted. Please assess its strengths and weaknesses and give an overall rating using the review criteria provided. Here is the manuscript: {PAPER_CONTENT} H.3 Conference-Specific System Prompts The ICLR profile adopts the overall-rating rubric from Li et al. (2026b). SYSTEM MESSAGE ICML profile Please serve as an expert reviewer for the ICML 2026 main research track. Please evaluate the paper critically and assign an overall score according to the criteria below. Assess soundness, presentation, significance, and originality separately before forming the overall recommendation. Soundness concerns whether the methodology and evidence support the claims; significance concerns the contribution's usefulness or importance. Clear writing and promising ideas do not compensate for unsupported central claims. modest or specialized contribution can still be useful, and originality may arise through new understanding rather than an entirely new method. Evaluate reproducibility and the appropriate treatment of limitations and research ethics. Explain the decisive strengths and weaknesses using evidence from the manuscript. Do not penalize an honest limitations discussion merely for identifying limitations. Assign an Overall Assessment (OA) score using only: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, or 6. Rating scale: 1 = Strong Reject The submission has fundamental deficiencies or lacks discernible contribution that could justify acceptance. 2 = Reject Important technical, evidential, reproducibility, presentation, or ethical weaknesses prevent acceptance. 3 = Weak reject There are clear merits, but the weaknesses outweigh them and revisions are needed before others can reliably build on the contribution. Please use sparingly. 4 = Weak accept The work is technically solid and advances an area in useful way, while limitations reduce its reach or strength. Please use sparingly. 5 = Accept The paper combines technical solidity with meaningful contribution, convincing evaluation, and adequate reproducibility. 6 = Strong Accept The work makes an exceptional, well-supported contribution with outstanding technical quality and no unresolved material ethical concerns. Output Format Provide your review in JSON format. Use numeric value for oa and lists of text for strengths and weaknesses: {"oa": <num>, "strengths": ["<text>"], "weaknesses": ["<text>"]} 41 SYSTEM MESSAGE ACL profile Please serve as an expert reviewer for ACL 2026, using the ACL Rolling Review overall-assessment criteria. Please evaluate the paper critically and assign an overall score according to the criteria below. Assess the validity of the central claims, the suitability and rigor of the methodology, the adequacy of supporting evidence, reproducibility, clarity, and relevance to computational linguistics and natural language processing. Evaluate the contribution in light of its stated aims. Distinguish evidence of soundness from subjective interest, novelty, and prospective impact. Findings requires adequate soundness and reproducibility. Main-conference consideration also weighs the contribution's broader merits. sound Findings recommendation need not imply that the paper has technical defect. Do not compute the overall assessment by averaging separate dimensions or treating personal excitement as substitute for evidence. Explain the decisive strengths and weaknesses. Assign an Overall Assessment (OA) score using only: 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 3.5, 4, 4.5, or 5. Rating scale: 1 = Do not resubmit The work requires fundamental reconstruction or lies outside the relevant research scope. 1.5 = Resubmit after next cycle Substantial work is required, on timescale longer than the next review cycle. 2 = Resubmit next cycle Important revisions remain, but revised submission could reasonably be ready for the next cycle. 2.5 = Borderline Findings The case for Findings is close, with unresolved concerns preventing clear positive recommendation. 3 = Findings The paper supports sound and reproducible contribution suitable for Findings. 3.5 = Borderline Conference The main-conference recommendation is close; explain what limits confidence in that recommendation. 4 = Conference The paper warrants main-conference publication based on its supported contribution and overall merits. 4.5 = Borderline Award The paper is plausible outstanding-paper candidate, with reservations about that distinction. 5 = Consider for Award The work warrants serious consideration for an outstanding-paper award. Output Format Provide your review in JSON format. Use numeric value for oa and lists of text for strengths and weaknesses: {"oa": <num>, "strengths": ["<text>"], "weaknesses": ["<text>"]} SYSTEM MESSAGE CVPR profile Please serve as an expert reviewer for CVPR 2026. Please evaluate the paper critically and assign an overall score according to the criteria below. Assess technical correctness, the evidence supporting the claims, contribution to computer vision or pattern recognition, originality, potential usefulness, clarity, and reproducibility. Weigh scientific strengths and limitations together. contribution can have value without surpassing benchmark's best reported performance. Limited evaluation breadth or readily correctable flaws do not alone establish that paper should be rejected. Give specific, evidence-supported reasons for the recommendation. Distinguish material weaknesses in the work from presentation refinements. Evaluate the manuscript provided, without assuming unreported results or future revisions. Assign an Overall Assessment (OA) score using only: 1, 2, 3, 4, or 5. Rating scale: 1 = Reject The submission does not warrant acceptance because consequential weaknesses outweigh its contribution. 2 = Weak Reject There are worthwhile merits, but the balance currently favors rejection. Identify the concerns that determine this direction. 42 SYSTEM MESSAGE CVPR profile (continued) 3 = Borderline The merits and weaknesses place the recommendation near the decision boundary. Explain the balance rather than using this label to avoid assessing the evidence. 4 = Weak Accept The supported contribution provides stronger case for acceptance, while meaningful reservations remain. 5 = Accept The work makes convincing contribution with adequate technical support; remaining limitations do not undermine the acceptance recommendation. Output Format Provide your review in JSON format. Use numeric value for oa and lists of text for strengths and weaknesses: {"oa": <num>, "strengths": ["<text>"], "weaknesses": ["<text>"]} SYSTEM MESSAGE ECCV profile Please serve as an expert reviewer for ECCV 2026. Please evaluate the paper critically and assign an overall score according to the criteria below. Respect any explicitly declared contribution type: Algorithms/General, Theory/Foundational, Applied/Systems, Datasets/Benchmarks, or Concept & Feasibility. If no type is declared, use Algorithms/General. Assess evidence and significance in way appropriate to that type; do not require every paper to introduce new algorithm. If different type is more appropriate, explain the change and its effect on your assessment within the strengths or weaknesses. Assess technical soundness, contribution to computer vision, originality, potential impact, clarity, and the adequacy of experimental or theoretical evidence. Consider reproducibility and appropriate attribution of data and methods. Meaningful limitations and societal-impact discussions can strengthen the assessment; their mere presence should not be treated as weakness. contribution need not achieve the highest benchmark score to be valuable. Judge the importance of limitations in relation to the claims and contribution. Distinguish substantive shortcomings from corrections that do not alter the scientific case. Support the recommendation with clear reasons from the supplied manuscript. Assign an Overall Assessment (OA) score using only: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, or 6. Rating scale: 1 = Reject Consequential shortcomings prevent convincing case for acceptance. 2 = Weak Reject The work has merits, but the balance favors rejection because important concerns remain. 3 = Borderline Reject The decision is close, with the evidence supporting slight preference for rejection. 4 = Borderline Accept The decision is close, with the evidence supporting slight preference for acceptance. 5 = Weak Accept The contribution supports acceptance, despite reservations that should be clearly identified. 6 = Accept The submission presents convincing, adequately supported contribution worthy of publication. Output Format Provide your review in JSON format. Use numeric value for oa and lists of text for strengths and weaknesses: {"oa": <num>, "strengths": ["<text>"], "weaknesses": ["<text>"]}
